q: The names of most enzymes are formed by adding which suffix to the name of the substrate or reaction?
x: Most enzymes are named by adding '-ase', as in maltase (acts on maltose) and lipase (acts on lipids). The ending '-ose' is used for sugars.

q: Most enzyme names end in '-ase'. Which of the following enzymes is an exception to this naming rule?
x: Pepsin, like trypsin and rennin, kept an older name that does not end in '-ase'. Lipase, maltase and sucrase follow the usual rule.

q: A few RNA molecules can also catalyse chemical reactions. Such catalytic RNA molecules are called:
x: Ribozymes are RNA molecules with catalytic activity; they are the main exception to the rule that enzymes are proteins. An apoenzyme is the protein part of a conjugated enzyme.

q: A single catalase molecule can break down millions of hydrogen peroxide molecules every second. This shows that enzymes are:
x: Enzymes work extremely fast and are not consumed, so one molecule can convert huge numbers of substrate molecules. They lower, not raise, activation energy.

q: Compared with its substrate, an enzyme molecule is usually:
o: Much larger, with only a small part forming the active site
Much smaller, so that it fits inside the substrate
About the same size, binding along its whole surface
x: Enzymes are large globular proteins, while most substrates are small molecules. Only a small region, the active site, actually binds the substrate.

q: Carbonic anhydrase speeds up the formation of carbonic acid from carbon dioxide and water in the tissues, and its breakdown in the lungs. This shows that an enzyme:
o: Can work in one direction only
Changes the products of the reaction
Can catalyse a reversible reaction in either direction
Is used up in the lungs
x: An enzyme speeds up both directions of a reversible reaction; the direction taken depends on the concentrations of reactants and products.

q: Which of the following is an intracellular enzyme?
x: Glycolytic enzymes act inside the cell, in the cytoplasm. Pepsin, pancreatic lipase and salivary amylase are secreted and act outside the cells that make them.

q: The hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out organelles inside a cell are packed in:
x: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs of hydrolytic enzymes used in intracellular digestion. Peroxisomes contain oxidative enzymes such as catalase, not the main digestive hydrolases.

q: Carbonic anhydrase contains zinc ions that are essential for its activity. In this enzyme, zinc acts as:
x: Metal ions such as Zn²⁺ that an enzyme needs to work are inorganic cofactors. A coenzyme is an organic cofactor, and the apoenzyme is the protein part.

q: In the small intestine, inactive trypsinogen is converted into active trypsin by:
x: Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) from the intestinal lining activates trypsinogen. Hydrochloric acid activates pepsinogen in the stomach, not trypsinogen.

q: Protein-digesting enzymes such as pepsin and trypsin are secreted in an inactive form mainly to:
o: Make them work faster at low pH
Let them pass through membranes as lipids
Protect the cells that make them from being digested
x: If they were active inside the cells that make them, these proteases would digest the cells' own proteins. They are activated only in the gut.

q: A deficiency of certain B-group vitamins slows many metabolic reactions. The reason is that:
o: These vitamins are the substrates of those reactions
Coenzymes are made from these vitamins, so the enzymes that need them cannot work
x: Many coenzymes, such as NAD⁺ and FAD, are built from B-group vitamins. Without the coenzyme, the apoenzyme is inactive.

q: Two enzymes each need an organic cofactor. After dialysis, which removes small molecules, enzyme X loses its activity but enzyme Y does not. The most likely explanation is that:
o: X has a prosthetic group, while Y uses a coenzyme
X uses a coenzyme, while Y has a prosthetic group
Both have tightly bound prosthetic groups
x: A coenzyme is loosely attached and is removed by dialysis, leaving an inactive apoenzyme. A prosthetic group is tightly bound and stays with the enzyme.

q: Chloride ions increase the activity of salivary amylase. Here chloride is acting as:
x: Small inorganic ions that increase an enzyme's activity are called activators; chloride ions activate salivary amylase. An inhibitor would reduce activity.

q: Enzymes extracted from cells can still catalyse their reactions in a test tube. This shows that enzymes:
o: Need an intact cell membrane to work
Can act independently of the living cell
x: Enzymes are made by living cells but are only proteins; given suitable conditions they work outside the cell too. This is why digestive enzymes work in the gut cavity.

q: Enzymes in living cells catalyse:
x: Enzymes control all of metabolism, from synthesis of proteins and DNA to the breakdown of food and respiratory substrates.

q: Which property is shared by enzymes AND inorganic catalysts?
o: Both speed up reactions without being used up
x: All catalysts speed up reactions and are left unchanged. Only enzymes are proteins, are destroyed by heat and show high specificity.

q: Because enzymes are proteins, the information needed to make each enzyme is carried by:
o: A gene in the cell's DNA
x: A gene codes for the amino acid sequence of the enzyme's polypeptide, which folds into its shape and active site.

q: Amylase digests starch but cannot digest cellulose, although both are polymers of glucose. This is because:
o: Amylase can only work inside plant cells
Cellulose molecules are smaller than starch molecules
The glucose units are joined by different linkages, and only the starch linkage fits amylase's active site
x: Starch has alpha linkages and cellulose has beta linkages. Amylase's active site fits only the alpha linkage, an example of enzyme specificity.

q: Which statement about cofactors is correct?
o: All cofactors are permanently bound to their enzymes
All cofactors are made of RNA
A cofactor may be an inorganic ion or an organic molecule
x: Cofactors are non-protein helpers: inorganic ions such as Mg²⁺ or Zn²⁺, or organic molecules (coenzymes and prosthetic groups). Some are loose, others tightly bound.

q: In many reactions, a coenzyme helps the enzyme by:
o: Forming the protein of the active site
Supplying amino acids for the enzyme
Carrying atoms or groups, such as hydrogen, from one reaction to another
x: Coenzymes act as carriers; for example, NAD⁺ picks up hydrogen in one reaction and passes it on in another.

q: In germinating seeds, stored starch is converted into maltose by the enzyme:
x: Amylase hydrolyses starch into maltose, supplying sugar to the growing embryo. Lipase acts on fats and pepsin on proteins.

q: Which of the following is NOT a cofactor?
x: The apoenzyme is the protein part of the enzyme itself. Coenzymes, prosthetic groups and metal ions are the non-protein cofactors it may need.

q: On an energy graph of a reaction, the activation energy is shown by the:
o: Difference between the energy of the reactants and the products
Difference between the energy of the reactants and the top of the curve
x: Activation energy is the energy barrier: the rise from the reactants' energy to the peak. The difference between reactants and products is the energy released or absorbed.

q: The catalytic action of an enzyme's active site is mainly due to:
o: The peptide bonds of the whole enzyme
Phosphate groups attached to the enzyme
The side chains (R groups) of particular amino acids lining it
Water molecules trapped in the enzyme
x: The R groups of the active-site amino acids give it its shape and chemical properties, which hold the substrate and help break or form its bonds.

q: After the enzyme–substrate complex has formed, the next step is that:
o: The substrate is changed into product while still bound, forming an enzyme–product complex
The enzyme is copied to form a new enzyme
The enzyme turns into a coenzyme
x: The sequence is E + S → ES → EP → E + P: the substrate is converted on the enzyme, and then the products are released.

q: The substance on which an enzyme acts is called its:
x: The substrate binds to the active site and is changed into products. A cofactor helps the enzyme, and an inhibitor slows it.

q: At any one moment, a single active site normally holds:
o: Only one substrate molecule (or one set of reacting molecules)
x: Each active site binds one substrate (or one set of reactants) at a time, converts it and releases the products before binding again.

q: An enzyme–substrate complex is not always converted into products. It can also:
o: Break apart into free enzyme and unchanged substrate
x: Binding is by weak bonds and is reversible, so some complexes simply separate again before any reaction happens.

q: When lipase hydrolyses a fat, the other reactant used in the reaction is:
x: Hydrolysis means splitting with water: water is added across each ester bond, giving glycerol and fatty acids.

q: Enzymes that join small molecules into larger ones during synthesis usually do so by:
x: Building large molecules such as proteins and polysaccharides involves condensation reactions, in which a molecule of water is removed at each bond formed.

q: Like finding an easier route over a mountain, an enzyme makes a reaction faster by:
o: Supplying extra energy to the reactants
Raising the temperature of the cell
Providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
Increasing the energy released by the reaction
x: The enzyme does not add energy; it offers a pathway with a lower energy barrier, so more molecules can react at body temperature.

q: Hydrogen peroxide can be made to break down faster either by heating it or by adding catalase. The difference between the two methods is that:
o: Heating gives more molecules enough energy to cross the barrier, while catalase lowers the barrier itself
Both methods lower the activation energy
Heating lowers the activation energy, while catalase raises the energy of the molecules
Both methods raise the energy of the products
x: Heat increases the kinetic energy of molecules so more exceed the activation energy. An enzyme instead reduces the activation energy needed.

q: The amino acids that make up an enzyme's active site:
o: Are often far apart in the polypeptide chain but are brought together by folding
Always lie next to each other in the chain
Are found only at the two ends of the chain
Are all the same amino acid
x: The active site is formed by the three-dimensional folding of the chain, so amino acids from distant parts of the sequence come together to form it.

q: In a metabolic pathway A → B → C → D:
o: One enzyme catalyses all the steps
Enzymes are needed only for the first step
The end product D acts as the enzyme for every step
Each step is catalysed by its own specific enzyme
x: Because enzymes are specific, each step of a pathway generally needs a different enzyme.

q: An enzyme catalyses the reversible reaction A ⇌ B. The enzyme lowers the activation energy of:
o: Both the forward and the reverse reaction
Neither reaction, but raises the product's energy
x: The energy barrier between the two compounds is the same peak approached from either side, so lowering it speeds up both directions.

q: A mutation alters only the catalytic site of an enzyme; its binding site is normal. The most likely result is that:
o: The substrate still binds but is not converted into products
The substrate can no longer bind
The enzyme works faster than before
x: The binding site attaches the substrate, but the catalytic site does the chemical change. With a faulty catalytic site the substrate is held but not changed.

q: Salivary amylase acting on starch produces mainly:
x: Amylase breaks starch into the disaccharide maltose; maltase later splits maltose into glucose. Glucose and fructose come from sucrose.

q: Sucrase hydrolyses one molecule of sucrose into:
x: Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose. Two glucose units come from maltose, and glucose plus galactose from lactose.

q: The lock-and-key model is most useful in explaining:
o: Why an enzyme acts on only one specific substrate
Why enzymes are denatured by heat
Why the active site changes shape during binding
x: In this model a rigid active site fits only one exactly matching substrate, just as one lock fits one key. Shape change on binding is the idea of induced fit.

q: Koshland's model is called 'induced fit' because:
o: The enzyme causes the substrate to be made
Heat causes the enzyme to fit the substrate
Binding of the substrate causes a change in the shape of the active site
The cofactor causes the enzyme to be made
x: In this model the active site is flexible; the substrate 'induces' the site to mould itself more closely around it.

q: Pepsin digests proteins by hydrolysing their:
x: Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, which proteases such as pepsin break with water. Glycosidic bonds link sugars and ester bonds occur in fats.

q: An enzyme converts glucose-6-phosphate into fructose-6-phosphate, which has the same atoms arranged differently. This shows that enzymes can:
o: Rearrange atoms within a single molecule
Only add oxygen to a molecule
x: Besides splitting and joining molecules, some enzymes (isomerases) rearrange a molecule into an isomer with the same formula.

q: An enzyme can make a reaction go faster in several ways. Which of these is NOT one of them?
o: Bringing reacting molecules close together in the right orientation
Providing a suitable chemical environment at the active site
Supplying energy to the substrate molecules
x: Enzymes lower activation energy by positioning, straining and providing a favourable environment; they do not supply energy.

q: The large part of an enzyme molecule outside its active site mainly:
o: Holds the active site in its correct three-dimensional shape
x: Only a few amino acids form the active site; the rest of the folded protein keeps the active site in the precise shape needed for binding and catalysis.

q: The breakdown of hydrogen peroxide can occur with no catalyst, with colloidal platinum, or with catalase. Which ranking of the activation energy, from highest to lowest, is correct?
o: Catalase, then platinum, then no catalyst
No catalyst, then platinum, then catalase
Platinum, then no catalyst, then catalase
Platinum, then catalase, then no catalyst
x: Any catalyst lowers the activation energy, but enzymes lower it far more than inorganic catalysts. So the uncatalysed reaction has the highest barrier and the catalase reaction the lowest.

q: Between about 0 °C and 40 °C, the rate of many enzyme-controlled reactions roughly:
o: Halves for every 10 °C rise in temperature
Doubles for every 10 °C rise in temperature
x: Below the optimum, a 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate (a temperature coefficient of about 2), because molecules move faster and collide more often.

q: Using the rule that the rate of an enzyme reaction doubles for each 10 °C rise, a reaction going at 5 units at 10 °C will go at about how many units at 30 °C (still below the optimum)?
x: From 10 to 20 °C the rate doubles to 10 units, and from 20 to 30 °C it doubles again to 20 units.

q: Bacteria that live in hot springs have enzymes that:
o: Have high optimum temperatures and are not denatured at those temperatures
x: Enzymes of such heat-loving (thermophilic) bacteria have very stable structures, so they keep their shape and work best at high temperatures.

q: Which of these enzymes has the highest optimum pH?
x: Arginase works best at about pH 9.7, which is strongly alkaline. Pepsin's optimum is about 2, salivary amylase about 6.8 and catalase about 7.6.

q: One enzyme sample is moved slightly away from its optimum pH, and another is put in a very strong acid. Which description of the outcome is right?
o: Any change of pH from the optimum denatures the enzyme permanently
pH has no effect on enzymes
A small change from the optimum lowers activity reversibly, but extreme pH denatures the enzyme
A small change from the optimum always increases activity
x: Slight pH changes alter charges and reduce activity, and returning to the optimum restores it. Extreme pH breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's shape, causing denaturation.

q: In an experiment, samples of a starch and amylase mixture are tested with iodine at intervals. The end point of digestion is reached when iodine:
o: No longer turns blue-black, showing the starch is used up
x: Iodine turns blue-black with starch. When all the starch has been digested, the sample stays yellow-brown, the colour of the iodine itself.

q: Starch solution is mixed with saliva that was boiled and then cooled, and kept at 37 °C for 30 minutes. When tested with iodine, the mixture will:
o: Stay yellow-brown, because the starch has been digested
Turn blue-black, because the boiled amylase cannot digest the starch
Stay yellow-brown, because boiling made the amylase more active
Turn colourless, because the iodine is destroyed
x: Boiling denatures salivary amylase permanently, so even after cooling the starch remains and gives the blue-black colour.

q: Buffer solutions are used in enzyme experiments in order to:
x: A buffer resists pH changes, so pH does not vary during the experiment and does not affect the results.

q: Which correctly matches a digestive enzyme with the conditions in which it works in the gut?
o: Salivary amylase – strongly alkaline small intestine
x: Pepsin works best near pH 2 in the stomach. Trypsin and pancreatic lipase need the alkaline small intestine, and salivary amylase works near neutral in the mouth.

q: Seeds sown in very cold soil germinate slowly mainly because:
o: Their enzymes are denatured by the cold
Their enzymes work very slowly at low temperature
Their starch is converted into protein
x: Low temperature reduces the kinetic energy of molecules, so enzyme reactions such as starch digestion in the seed are slow. The enzymes are not denatured.

q: Vegetables are often dipped briefly in boiling water (blanched) before freezing. This is done to:
o: Denature the vegetables' own enzymes, which would otherwise slowly spoil them
Add extra enzymes to the vegetables
Raise the pH of the vegetables
x: Freezing only slows enzymes, it does not destroy them. Brief heating denatures them so the food keeps its colour and taste longer.

q: An enzyme's rate was measured at substrate concentrations of 1, 2, 4 and 8 mM, giving 10, 20, 35 and 36 units. Between 4 and 8 mM, the rate is limited mainly by:
o: A temperature that is too high
A pH that is too low
x: Doubling substrate from 4 to 8 mM barely changes the rate, so the active sites are nearly all occupied; the amount of enzyme now limits the rate.

q: An enzyme has an optimum temperature because:
o: Rising temperature increases collisions but also increases denaturation, and the balance gives the highest rate at the optimum
The enzyme stops moving at the optimum
Activation energy rises as temperature rises
The substrate is denatured above the optimum
x: Up to a point, faster molecular movement speeds the reaction. Beyond it, denaturation of enzyme molecules outweighs this, so the rate falls.

q: Egg white turns solid and white when boiled. The change in an enzyme that is similar to this is:
o: Denaturation of its protein by heat
x: Egg white is mostly protein; heat breaks the weak bonds holding its shape, just as heat denatures an enzyme. The amino acid chain itself is not hydrolysed.

q: Which of the following does NOT denature an enzyme?
x: Low temperature only slows an enzyme, and activity returns on warming. Heat and extremes of pH destroy its three-dimensional shape.

q: An enzyme reaction has plenty of enzyme but very little substrate. Which change would increase the rate the most?
o: Moving the pH away from the optimum
x: With few substrate molecules, most active sites are empty, so extra enzyme helps little. Extra substrate fills more active sites and raises the rate.

q: An enzyme is added to a fixed, small amount of substrate. If the experiment is repeated with twice as much enzyme, then:
o: Twice as much product forms in total
Half as much product forms in total
The same total amount of product forms, but in a shorter time
x: The total product depends on the substrate available, which is unchanged. More enzyme only makes the reaction finish sooner.

q: Two enzymes have activity curves that peak at pH 2 and pH 8 respectively. These enzymes are most likely:
x: Pepsin of the acidic stomach works best near pH 2, while trypsin of the small intestine works best in slightly alkaline conditions near pH 8.

q: A change of pH can slow an enzyme reaction even when the enzyme's shape is not changed, because:
o: The charges on the substrate may change, so it binds less well to the active site
pH changes the temperature of the mixture
pH increases the amount of substrate
pH always breaks the peptide bonds of the substrate
x: Binding depends on matching charges on both the enzyme and the substrate. If pH changes the substrate's ionisation, binding and reaction rate fall.

q: The rate of an enzyme reaction is measured as the:
o: Amount of product formed, or substrate used, per unit time
x: Rate means how fast the reaction proceeds: how much product appears, or substrate disappears, in a given time.

q: In an investigation of the effect of temperature on amylase, which factors must be kept the same in every tube?
o: Only the volume of iodine used
No factors need to be kept the same
pH and the concentrations of enzyme and starch
x: Only temperature should vary; pH, enzyme and substrate concentrations are kept constant so that any change in rate is due to temperature alone.

q: The optimum pH of most enzymes that work inside human cells is close to:
x: The cytoplasm is close to neutral, and most intracellular enzymes work best near pH 7. Pepsin, with an optimum near 2, is an exception suited to the stomach.

q: In some enzyme experiments, tubes are placed in ice at a chosen time. This is done to:
o: Stop the reaction at that time without destroying the enzyme
x: At very low temperature enzyme activity almost stops, but the enzyme is not denatured. This 'freezes' the reaction at a known moment.

q: Heavy metal ions such as mercury (Hg²⁺) and lead (Pb²⁺) inhibit enzymes mainly by:
o: Binding to sulphur-containing (–SH) groups and changing the enzyme's shape
Raising the pH of the cell
x: These metal ions combine with –SH groups of the enzyme's amino acids, distorting its shape. This is why they are poisonous.

q: Some nerve gases and organophosphate insecticides are deadly because they:
o: Act as cofactors for nerve enzymes
Increase the activity of nerve enzymes
x: These poisons bind permanently to acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine is not broken down and nerve impulses go out of control.

q: The antibiotic penicillin kills bacteria by:
o: Denaturing all bacterial proteins by heat
Acting as a coenzyme for bacteria
Inhibiting an enzyme that bacteria need to build their cell walls
x: Penicillin blocks a bacterial enzyme that makes cross-links in the cell wall. Without a strong wall the bacteria burst.

q: Penicillin harms bacteria but not human cells mainly because:
o: Human cells have no cell wall, so they lack the enzyme it targets
x: An inhibitor acts only on its target enzyme. The wall-building enzyme blocked by penicillin is not present in human cells.

q: Sulpha drugs (sulphonamides) have a shape very like PABA, a substance bacteria use to make folic acid. These drugs act on the bacterial enzyme as:
x: A molecule that resembles the substrate and competes with it for the active site is a competitive inhibitor.

q: The effect of a non-competitive inhibitor on an enzyme reaction is similar to:
o: Raising the temperature to the optimum
Reducing the amount of working enzyme
x: A non-competitive inhibitor puts some enzyme molecules out of action whatever the substrate level, just as if less enzyme were present.

q: Increasing the concentration of an inhibitor, with other conditions unchanged, usually:
o: Turns the inhibitor into an activator
x: More inhibitor molecules bind more enzyme molecules, so the reaction slows further.

q: In feedback inhibition, the end product can inhibit the first enzyme of the pathway even though it has a different shape from that enzyme's substrate. This is possible because:
o: It has exactly the same shape as the substrate
It binds at a separate allosteric site, not the active site
It increases the amount of substrate
x: The end product does not compete for the active site. It binds a regulatory (allosteric) site, which changes the shape of the active site.

q: During non-competitive inhibition, can the substrate and the inhibitor occupy one enzyme molecule simultaneously?
o: No, because they compete for the active site
No, because the inhibitor destroys the enzyme first
Yes, because they bind at different sites
Yes, because the inhibitor is identical to the substrate
x: A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere on the enzyme, so the substrate can still occupy the active site, but it is converted poorly or not at all.

q: The substrate concentration is 100 times that of a competitive inhibitor with similar binding strength. The inhibition will be:
x: Competitive inhibition depends on the relative amounts of substrate and inhibitor. With a large excess of substrate, most active sites hold substrate.

q: When an end product switches off its own pathway, the type of control involved is:
x: A rise in the end product switches off its own production, and a fall allows production to resume: a negative feedback loop.

q: Naturally occurring enzyme inhibitors in cells help to:
x: Cells use inhibition, such as feedback inhibition, to switch pathways on and off so that products are made only when needed.

q: A competitive inhibitor attaches to the enzyme:
o: Reversibly, at an allosteric site only
x: Competitive inhibitors occupy the active site by weak bonds and can leave again, which is why excess substrate can displace them.

q: Which is the correct order of events in non-competitive inhibition?
o: Substrate binds → inhibitor joins the active site → products form → enzyme is freed
Inhibitor binds the active site → substrate is displaced → enzyme is denatured → products form
Inhibitor binds at another site → enzyme changes shape → active site is distorted → substrate is not converted
Active site is distorted → inhibitor binds at another site → enzyme changes shape → substrate is converted
x: The non-competitive inhibitor first binds away from the active site; the resulting shape change distorts the active site so the substrate cannot be converted.

q: An enzyme–inhibitor complex formed with a competitive inhibitor:
x: While the inhibitor occupies the active site, no substrate can bind there, so no product is formed by that enzyme molecule.

q: A competitive inhibitor binds more strongly to the active site than the substrate does. To overcome its effect:
o: A much higher substrate concentration is needed
A lower substrate concentration is needed
Nothing can overcome it, even in theory
The temperature must be raised far above the optimum
x: Competitive inhibition can be overcome by excess substrate, but the stronger the inhibitor binds, the more substrate is needed to win the competition.

q: Molecules that bind to an enzyme's allosteric site can:
o: Either increase or decrease the enzyme's activity
x: The allosteric site is a regulatory site. Binding of an inhibitor there lowers activity, while binding of an activator raises it.

q: In feedback inhibition, the end product usually inhibits the first enzyme of the pathway rather than the last one because:
o: The last enzyme has no active site
This stops the whole pathway early, so raw materials and intermediates are not wasted
Inhibition of the first enzyme is always irreversible
The end product has the same shape as the first substrate
x: Blocking the first step prevents intermediates from piling up and saves the starting material for other uses.

q: Enzyme inhibitors can be divided into two broad groups:
x: Reversible inhibitors bind by weak bonds and can leave the enzyme; irreversible inhibitors bind permanently, often by covalent bonds.

q: An irreversible inhibitor forms a covalent bond with an amino acid in an enzyme's active site. Adding a large amount of substrate will:
x: Covalently bound inhibitors cannot be displaced by substrate, so the affected enzyme molecules stay inactive.

q: A drug designed to block an enzyme by fitting into its active site is usually made to resemble:
o: The product of a different enzyme
x: To occupy the active site, a competitive inhibitor must have a shape and charge similar to the substrate.

q: In a pathway A → B → C, product C inhibits the first enzyme by feedback. A mutation makes this enzyme's allosteric site unable to bind C. The result is that:
o: C is overproduced, because the pathway is no longer switched off
No C can be made at all
The first enzyme can no longer bind A
x: The active site is unaffected, so the pathway still runs, but C can no longer switch off the first enzyme, so C keeps being made even when plentiful.
